name: m365
description: Microsoft 365 — read and manage SharePoint, Teams, Entra ID and Outlook through the CLI for Microsoft 365.

settings.label: Sign-in mode
settings.description: How this plugin signs in. Exactly one mode is in force: Authenticate signs out first and then uses this one, and the plugin counts as signed in only while the stored connection matches what is set here — change it and the plugin reads as signed out until you authenticate again. Each mode needs different fields below; the ones the other mode uses are ignored.

options.label: Device code (sign in as a person)
options.description: A human completes the login in a browser and the server acts as that account, with that account's permissions. Needs an app registration with 'Allow public client flows' enabled and delegated permissions. The sign-in expires with its refresh token, so it has to be repeated eventually.

options.label: Certificate (sign in as the application)
options.description: App-only: no user is involved, so nothing expires until the certificate does and nobody has to be present. The app registration needs APPLICATION permissions with admin consent — delegated ones do nothing here — and commands that mean 'the signed-in user' (a personal mailbox, a OneDrive, 'me') have no account to resolve.

settings.label: Entra app (client) ID
settings.description: The application (client) ID of the Entra app registration this server signs in with. Needed by both sign-in modes. CLI for Microsoft 365 v10+ has no shared default app, so sign-in cannot proceed without one. Create it once with `m365 setup` on a workstation, or in the Azure portal, and paste the id here.

settings.label: Tenant
settings.description: Tenant to authenticate against. `common` works only for a MULTI-tenant app registration signing in by device code; a single-tenant one needs your tenant's GUID here, or sign-in fails with AADSTS7000014 ("device_code is not valid") and never shows a code at all. Certificate sign-in is always tenant-specific and REFUSES `common` outright. If in doubt, use the GUID.

secrets.label: Certificate, base64-encoded (certificate mode)
secrets.description: The .pfx or .pem holding the certificate and its private key, base64-encoded: `base64 -w0 cert.pfx`. The only way it is supplied, deliberately — a path to a file on the server would be a second channel saying the same thing, and it would need shell access on this box to be any use, which pasting does not. Write-only: encrypted at rest and never read back. Not marked required, because it is only needed in certificate mode; the sign-in says so plainly if it is missing.

secrets.label: Certificate password (certificate mode)
secrets.description: The password protecting the private key, if it has one — a .pfx exported from Windows normally does. Leave empty for an unprotected key. It is never passed on a command line: the sign-in opens the certificate with it locally and hands the CLI an already-opened copy, which is why openssl is a requirement for a protected certificate.
